newsitem.title: USA: Ford May U.S. sales fell, capping slow month.
newsitem.headline: Ford May U.S. sales fell, capping slow month.

text.p: Ford Motor Co. Wednesday reported a 3 percent decline in May U.S. car and light-truck sales, with lower car sales offsetting a record performance in light trucks.
The Ford results -- comparatively better than those of Chrysler Corp. and General Motors Corp. -- capped a second consecutive month of slower industry sales.
Ford said domestic car sales fell 11.8 percent to 150,185 units while light-truck sales, fueled by strong demand for sport utility vehicles, rose 5.2 percent to 206,087.

Overall, industry sales fell 5.7 percent to 1.4 million units in May, which was good enough for a seasonally adjusted annual sales rate of about 14.9 million units, an improvement from April's 14.3 million units. May 1996 industry sales ran at a 15.4 million annual rate.
Last months' rate also was significantly below the first-quarter rate of about 15.6 million units, which analysts had said was unsustainable, given high levels of consumer debt.

"Sales are a little weaker than expected, but they aren't falling off the table," PaineWebber Inc. analyst Michael Ward said. "Looking at the year as a whole, I don't see anything that will prevent us from getting to 14.8 million to 15 million units."
Domestic vehicle sales totaled 15.1 million units in 1996.
Ford's sales declines were below the 16.6 percent overall May sales drop reported by Chrysler and the 8.1 percent drop reported by GM this week.
Ford continued to be bullish about light truck demand, and confirmed widely anticipated plans to add 15,000 trucks to its second-quarter production schedule.
As a result, Ford intends to build 772,000 trucks in the quarter, up 13 percent from a year earlier.
Spokesman George Pipas said the production increase was mainly in Ford's Windstar minivan line, which had a 6.6 percent May sales gain and is up 6.3 percent so far this year.
Ford also said it added 5,000 cars to its second-quarter schedules, which would put output at 466,000 cars, a 14 percent decline from the 541,000 cars it built a year ago.

GM's sales, hurt by two assembly plant strikes, included a 5.4 percent increase in truck sales and a 16.7 percent drop in car sales. Chrysler's car sales fell 17.9 percent, while truck sales, hurt by an engine plant strike, fell 15.5 percent.
"It isn't raining as hard here as it is in Auburn Hills," a Ford official said, referring to Chrysler's suburban Detroit headquarters city.
Ford boasted another new truck sales record, fueled largely by sport utility vehicles, especially the new, full-size Ford Expedition.

Ford said it sold a total of 58,879 sport utility vehicles during the month, up 47 percent over last year. Calendar year-to-date, Ford sport utility sales totaled 259,279 units, up 34 percent from last year.

Ford also plans on July 1 to introduce the new Lincoln Navigator luxury sport utility vehicle, which is based on the Expedition platform. The No. 2 U.S. automaker said it currently has dealer orders for nearly 11,000 Navigators.
Robert Rewey, Ford group vice president of marketing and sales, said industry sales were in line with Ford's expectations, despite softening in the last two months.

"As anticipated, the last couple of months haven't matched the first quarter's sales rate, but year-to-date sales are consistent with our full year forecast -- somewhere in the range of 15 to 15.5 million, about the same as last year," Rewey said in a statement.
